One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it.

articles.summary: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term. National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention. Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges. Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle . A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden would not have run for reelection in 2024 if he had known about his cancer, he said in an interview released Wednesday in which he also sought to downplay the historic debate performance that helped end his political career. "If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have not gone forward because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," he said in the interview with People magazine , which was conducted last week following Democrats’ big midterm wins and ahead of his upcoming memoir’s release. The former president announced his diagnosis — Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer — in May 2025, just four months after leaving the White House. It triggered an outpouring of public support — but it also raised questions about how doctors failed to catch the cancer earlier and whether it might have contributed to Biden’s apparent decline toward the end of his term. “I think it’s very sad, actually. I’m surprised that it wasn’t, you know, the public wasn’t notified a long time ago because to get to [a Gleason score of] 9, that’s a long time,” President Donald Trump told reporters shortly after Biden’s announcement.
